topic: The 90/180 Schengen Rule Now That EES Counts Your Days for You
metaTitle: The 90/180 Schengen Rule Now That EES Counts Your Days
metaDescription: The 90/180 rule has not changed, but EES now records every entry and exit digitally. How the rolling window works, with a worked example and the overstay rules.
excerpt: The 90 days in any 180-day period rule is old, but the enforcement is new. Since April 2026 the Entry/Exit System holds a digital record of every Schengen crossing, so missed stamps no longer buy you extra days. Here is how the rolling window actually counts, worked through with dates.
quickAnswer: You can spend 90 days in any rolling 180-day period across the Schengen area, and since 10 April 2026 the Entry/Exit System logs every crossing digitally instead of stamping your passport. Count back 180 days from each day of your stay. Your entry day and your exit day both count as full days, and the record stays on file for three years.
content:
The rule has not changed. You get 90 days inside any rolling 180-day period across the Schengen area, and that wording has been in the Schengen Borders Code since 2013. What changed is the counting: since 10 April 2026 the Entry/Exit System holds a digital record of every crossing, so the arithmetic is done for you and a missed or smudged stamp no longer works in your favour.

What does the 90/180 rule actually say?

It says you may stay no more than 90 days in any 180-day period, and that you work this out by looking back at the 180 days before each day of your stay. The European Commission's own user manual for the short-stay calculator spells out the mechanism: the word "any" means a moving 180-day reference period, checked backwards from the day of entry or the day an officer actually stops you.

Two details do most of the damage. The 180 days are not a calendar half-year that resets on a fixed date, and the 90 days are shared across all the Schengen countries, not counted per country.

At a glance

FactPositionSource

What you need to check your own count

  • Every entry date into the Schengen area over the past six months
  • Every matching exit date, including the day you flew home
  • Your visa sticker, if you hold one, because the days written on it can be fewer than 90
  • The intended entry date for your next trip
  • The Commission's short-stay calculator, in planning mode

What changed when EES replaced the passport stamp?

The enforcement, not the rule. Under the old system a border officer worked out your days from ink in your passport. Stamps were skipped on busy shifts, printed over each other, or left so faint nobody could read the date. Every one of those errors was a free day for the traveller.

EES removes that. The system registers your name, travel document data, fingerprints, facial image and the date and place of each entry and exit, and it flags overstayers automatically. The officer is no longer squinting at your passport. The screen already knows.

It went live on 12 October 2025 and was rolled out border post by border post over six months, so the transition was genuinely patchy for a while. The Commission confirmed the system was fully operational at all external border crossing points on 10 April 2026, with more than 52 million entries and exits registered during the rollout alone.

One practical consequence for anyone who travelled during that winter: your history may be part digital and part ink. If you crossed at a post that had not switched over yet, that trip sits in your passport rather than in the database, and it still counts.

How do I count a rolling 180-day window?

Pick the day you plan to be in Schengen, count back 180 days including that day, and add up every day you were inside the area during that stretch. If the total is over 90, you have a problem.

Here is a real-shaped example. Say you are a Dubai resident on a multi-entry C visa, and you want to fly to Vienna on 1 October 2026. Counting back 180 days from 1 October gives a window of 5 April 2026 to 1 October 2026.

TripDatesDays of stayFalls inside 5 Apr to 1 Oct 2026?Days that count
Paris5 to 24 March 202620No, it ended before 5 April0
Rome and Barcelona10 May to 8 June 202630Yes, all of it30
Total on 1 October 202630 of 90 used

So on 1 October you land with 60 days of headroom, even though you spent 50 days in Europe this year. The March trip has aged out of the window.

Note how those day counts are built. The Paris trip is 20 days, not 19, because the date of entry counts as the first day of stay and the date of exit counts as the last. A weekend break landing Friday and leaving Sunday burns three days, not one. Over a year of short city trips, that rounding is where people quietly lose a fortnight.

If you are building a Schengen file around this trip, the same dates need to appear on your flight reservation, which is exactly what a dummy ticket for a Schengen visa is for: a live booking that matches the plan you just worked out.

Why does my allowance grow while I am still in Europe?

Because the window keeps moving while you sit still. This is the part that trips up careful people, and it works in your favour rather than against you.

Carry on with the example. You entered on 1 October with 30 days already used, so the naive answer is that you must leave by 29 November. But check the count on 29 November itself: the 180-day window has slid forward to 3 June to 29 November. Only six days of the Rome and Barcelona trip, the 3rd to the 8th of June, are still inside it.

Day you check180-day windowOld days still countingDays of the current stayTotal
1 Oct 20265 Apr to 1 Oct30131
6 Nov 202611 May to 6 Nov293766
29 Nov 20263 Jun to 29 Nov66066

You are at 66, not 90. The old days fell out of the back of the window at the same rate you added new ones at the front. This is why guessing is a bad idea in both directions: people either overstay by accident or cut a trip short for no reason.

Run the dates through the Commission's short-stay calculator in planning mode rather than doing it on paper. The Commission is blunt that the calculator is a helping tool only and does not create a right to stay. The border officer makes the decision.

What happens if I overstay, and how long does the record last?

An overstay is not a fine you pay and forget. Staying beyond your authorised period makes your presence unlawful, and the Schengen Borders Code framework allows a return decision and an entry ban that can run up to five years, recorded in the Schengen Information System.

In practice the range is wide. A day or two may end with a warning at the airport. A longer overstay can mean refusal of entry next time, a ban, and a visa application that starts from a much worse place. Refusals of entry are themselves logged in EES.

The retention period is the part most people have not absorbed. Under the EES Regulation, your record is held for three years after your last entry, exit or refusal of entry, and for five years where there is no exit record following the end of your authorised stay. A summer you would rather forget is on file for the next three years of applications.

One thing EES does not do is change what a visa officer wants to see in your file. It just makes your travel history checkable in seconds.

Why do Schengen applications get refused over the day count?

Almost always for avoidable reasons, and almost all of them are consistency problems rather than day-count problems.

  • The dates on the form do not match the dates on the booking. The consulate reads both. A reservation that ends a week after your stated return raises a question you then have to answer.
  • The trip on paper would put you over 90 days. If your requested dates plus your recent history exceed the allowance, the application is answering its own refusal.
  • A previous overstay, now visible. This used to depend on whether an officer noticed a stamp. It no longer does.
  • An expired reservation. A booking that has lapsed by the time the file is opened cannot be verified, which is why the validity tier you buy matters more than the route.
  • Thin evidence of ties and funds. Neither a reservation nor a policy fixes this, and no document can. Refusals turn on funds, ties and a story that holds together.

Worth saying plainly: a reservation is a genuine booking held under a live PNR, not a forged ticket. Article 14 of the EU Visa Code asks for evidence of your travel arrangements, not proof that you have already paid a fare you may never fly. That is the whole reason a flight reservation for your Schengen file exists as a product.

What does it cost to put the paperwork together?

Two separate bills, and it helps to keep them separate in your head. The consulate fee is fixed by the EU. What you pay us is for the documents that go into the file.

faqs.question: Does the 180-day period reset on 1 January?
faqs.answer: No. There is no fixed reset date. The 180 days are counted backwards from whichever day you are checking, so the window moves forward one day at a time. Count back 180 days from your planned entry date and add up the days you spent inside Schengen.

faqs.question: Do my arrival and departure days both count as days of stay?
faqs.answer: Yes, both count in full. The date of entry is the first day of stay and the date of exit is the last. A trip landing on 5 March and leaving on 24 March is 20 days, not 19. A Friday to Sunday break costs you three days.

faqs.question: Does EES still stamp my passport?
faqs.answer: No. Since 10 April 2026 the Entry/Exit System has replaced stamping at all external Schengen border crossing points. Your entry and exit are recorded digitally along with fingerprints and a facial image. Trips made before the rollout finished may still sit in your passport as ink.

faqs.question: How long does an EES record stay on file?
faqs.answer: Three years from your last entry, exit or refusal of entry. Where an overstay is recorded and no exit follows the end of your authorised stay, the retention period is five years. A consulate reviewing your next application can see that history in seconds.

faqs.question: Do days spent in Ireland or Cyprus count towards my 90?
faqs.answer: No. Neither is part of the Schengen area without internal borders, so time there sits outside the count. Days in Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland do count, because those four are Schengen states even though they are not EU members.
